reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: an invented evaluation with seven weighted criteria: fit 25%, operational burden 15%, security and supply-chain risk 20%, integration 15%, support 10%, life-cycle cost 10% and exit risk 5%. Each vendor is scored from 1 to 10 on each criterion, and a security score below 5 disqualifies a vendor regardless of total.

Derivation: vendor X scores 9, 5, 4, 6, 7, 6 and 3, giving 0.25 × 9 + 0.15 × 5 + 0.20 × 4 + 0.15 × 6 + 0.10 × 7 + 0.10 × 6 + 0.05 × 3 = 6.15. Vendor Y scores 7, 8, 8, 8, 7, 7 and 7, giving 7.5. Judged only by fit, the demo winner X leads 9 to 7; judged on all criteria, Y leads 7.5 to 6.15.

Independent check: the weights add up to 100%, so each total is a true weighted average on the 1-to-10 scale. Vendor X also fails the security gate with a 4, so it would be excluded even if its total were higher.

Misconception to reject: 'the demo shows what we are buying.' A demo shows features under ideal conditions; operational burden, security practices, integration effort, support quality and exit cost appear only through questions, references and trials.

Change one factor: raise fit to 40% and cut security to 5%, keeping the other weights. X rises to 6.9 and Y falls to 7.35, so Y still leads, and the security gate still excludes X. A gate protects the decision from weights that drift toward the demo.

Source and limits: NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1, Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management Practices for Systems and Organizations (May 2022, updated November 2024), guides organizations in identifying, assessing and mitigating cybersecurity risks throughout the supply chain, including risk assessments for the products and services they acquire: https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-161r1-upd1. The weights, scores and gate are invented.

leadership-vendor-lockin.essentialQuestion: Before signing with a cloud provider, how do you estimate what leaving would cost, and how much of that cost would a legal ban on switching charges remove?

reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: an invented exit estimate for 400 TB of data. Provider-billed items: data transfer out at $0.05 per GB ($20,000) and an early-termination fee ($30,000). Internal items: 6 engineer-months of re-integration at $15,000 each ($90,000), retraining ($10,000) and 2 months of running both platforms at $25,000 a month ($50,000).

Derivation: 400 TB is 400,000 GB, and 400,000 × $0.05 = $20,000. The total exit cost is 20,000 + 30,000 + 90,000 + 10,000 + 50,000 = $200,000, of which $150,000, or 75%, is internal work that no provider bills.

Independent check: even if every provider-billed item disappeared, $150,000 of exit cost would remain. Lock-in therefore comes mostly from integrations, skills and operating processes, which you can reduce by design: portable data formats, standard interfaces and a tested export.

Misconception to reject: 'lock-in is only about the contract.' Contract terms matter, but the larger cost in this example is the work of moving, which grows every month that more systems depend on the provider's specific features.

Change one factor: with 2 PB instead of 400 TB, data transfer becomes 2,000,000 × $0.05 = $100,000, the total becomes $280,000 and the internal share falls to about 54%. For data-heavy systems, transfer charges matter more.

Source and limits: Article 29 of the EU Data Act, Regulation (EU) 2023/2854, says that from 12 January 2027 providers of data processing services shall not impose switching charges on customers, and that from 11 January 2024 to 12 January 2027 reduced switching charges may not exceed the provider's costs directly linked to the switch: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/2854/oj. Which charges count as switching charges, and whether a service is in scope, depends on the regulation's definitions, so check with counsel; all prices here are invented.
